reader_situation: People whose counters, chairs and stair steps fill up with things set down 'for now'. They've heard of the one-touch rule and want to know if it actually works, how long until it's automatic, and what to do with the items (especially mail) that can't be put away instantly.
direct_answer: The one-touch rule means putting an item where it belongs the first time you pick it up instead of setting it down for later. It works best tied to a fixed cue (walking in the door, finishing dinner) and repeated daily; habit research found automaticity plateaued after about 66 days on average, and an occasional missed day didn't derail it.
consensus: Clutter builds from many small 'I'll deal with it later' decisions.
Give every item a home before expecting yourself to put it away.
Use landing zones (trays, hooks) for true exceptions and empty them on a schedule.
Pair the rule with a weekly reset.
Mail should be handled immediately, not piled.
gaps: How long it takes: the common '21 days to form a habit' has no research basis (it traces to anecdotes about plastic-surgery patients); in Lally's study, automaticity plateaued after an average of 66 days, with considerable variation, and simple actions became automatic faster than elaborate routines.
Missed days: automaticity gains soon resumed after one missed performance, so a bad day doesn't reset the habit.

What makes it automatic: habits are actions triggered by contextual cues; the advice is to repeat the same action in the same context (time and place you meet every day), which means anchoring one-touch to specific cues like the front door rather than a general resolution.

Why 'I'll take it upstairs later' fails: Notre Dame psychologist Gabriel Radvansky found that walking through a doorway acts as an event boundary and makes decisions made in the other room harder to recall; the deferred second trip is easy to forget.

Mail needs a decision rule, not a tray: the FTC says shred documents with personal information before throwing them away (or black out account numbers), and to keep financial records and ID cards in a safe place; the IRS says keep records supporting a tax return 3 years in most cases, 7 years for worthless-securities or bad-debt claims, and property records until the limitations period runs out for the year you dispose of the property.

Visual clutter costs attention: Neuroscientists McMains and Kastner (Journal of Neuroscience, 2011) found that multiple visual stimuli compete for neural representation by mutually suppressing their activity in visual cortex (lab research, not a study of homes).
The old article's '15 seconds' threshold has no source and should go.

evidence.claim: Time for a daily action to become automatic
evidence.detail: Daily ratings of automaticity showed an asymptotic increase that slowed to a plateau after an average of 66 days; there was considerable variation across participants and behaviours. The authors suggest telling people to expect habit formation to take around 10 weeks.
evidence.source_title: Making health habitual: the psychology of 'habit-formation' and general practice | British Journal of General Practice (Gardner, Lally, Wardle, 2012)

evidence.claim: Missing a day and simple vs elaborate actions
evidence.detail: Missing the occasional opportunity to perform the behaviour did not seriously impair the habit formation process: automaticity gains soon resumed after one missed performance. Automaticity peaked more quickly for simple actions (drinking water) than for more elaborate routines (50 sit-ups).
evidence.source_title: Making health habitual: the psychology of 'habit-formation' and general practice | British Journal of General Practice (Gardner, Lally, Wardle, 2012)

evidence.claim: The 21-day myth and how habits form
evidence.detail: The popular claim that habits take 21 days appears to have originated from anecdotal evidence of plastic-surgery patients adjusting to their appearance within 21 days. Habits are actions triggered automatically in response to contextual cues associated with their performance; advice: repeat a chosen behaviour in the same context until it becomes automatic. Box 1: plan when and where; choose a time and place you encounter every day; you can't form a habit for not doing something, so pick an action to do rather than one to avoid.
evidence.source_title: Making health habitual: the psychology of 'habit-formation' and general practice | British Journal of General Practice (Gardner, Lally, Wardle, 2012)

evidence.claim: Doorways make deferred tasks easier to forget
evidence.detail: Radvansky argues a doorway acts as an 'event boundary'. In virtual and real-world experiments with college students, memory for objects was worse after passing through a doorway than after walking the same distance within one room; returning to the original room did not restore memory.
evidence.source_title: Walking through doorways causes forgetting, new research shows | University of Notre Dame News (Nov. 16, 2011)

evidence.claim: Visual items compete for the brain's attention
evidence.detail: Multiple stimuli compete for neural representation by mutually suppressing their evoked activity throughout visual cortex; attentional modulation was constrained by how much bottom-up processes had already resolved that competition.
evidence.source_title: Interactions of Top-Down and Bottom-Up Mechanisms in Human Visual Cortex | Journal of Neuroscience (McMains & Kastner, 2011)

evidence.claim: Handle mail with personal information promptly and shred it
evidence.detail: Take mail with personal information out of the mailbox as soon as possible. When you get rid of documents, shred them before throwing them away; without a shredder, use a local shred day or a marker to block out account numbers. Keep financial records, Social Security and Medicare cards in a safe place.
evidence.source_title: What To Know About Identity Theft | FTC Consumer Advice

evidence.claim: How long to keep tax-related papers
evidence.detail: Keep records 3 years in the general case; 3 years from filing or 2 years from paying (whichever is later) for refund claims; 7 years for a loss from worthless securities or bad debt deduction; 6 years if unreported income exceeds 25% of gross income; indefinitely if no return or a fraudulent return was filed. Keep property records until the period of limitations expires for the year you dispose of the property.
evidence.source_title: How long should I keep records? | Internal Revenue Service

real_questions: How long until putting things away right away becomes automatic?
What if I'm carrying something and the right place is upstairs?
What do I do with mail I can't deal with yet?
Does one bad week ruin the habit?
How do I get the rest of the household to do it?

original_asset.spec: A 'pick it up, then what?' decision flow: does it have a home -> is the home in this room (doorway effect, Notre Dame) -> if not, a single named landing spot emptied at a fixed daily cue; plus a mail flow (act now / file by IRS retention period / shred per FTC). Followed by a 10-week cue-based plan built on the BJGP Box 1 method (one cue, one simple action, same place daily; expect ~66 days on average, a missed day is fine).

cautions: Shred, don't toss, mail with account numbers or personal information.
Don't present the 66-day figure as a fixed deadline; it's an average with wide variation.
The visual-competition finding is lab neuroscience, not a home study.
